extraction.name: MathQA
extraction.description: A dataset of approximately 37,000 English multiple-choice math word problems derived from AQuA and annotated with interpretable operation programs. Its representation language contains 58 operations and covers geometry, physics, probability, gain-loss, general, and other categories. Table 1 reports 37,259 problems.
extraction.creator: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, and Hannaneh Hajishirzi
extraction.citeAs: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, and Hannaneh Hajishirzi. MathQA: Towards Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Operation-Based Formalisms. arXiv:1905.13319v1 [cs.CL], 30 May 2019.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The authors selected math word problems from the existing AQuA dataset and used crowdsourcing to align them with formal operation programs. Problems were first categorized into mathematical domains using term frequencies to constrain the available operations. Annotations were also expanded to closely similar AQuA problems using a Levenshtein-distance threshold of four words.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The source AQuA dataset contains rationales with few or none of the required solution steps. The authors report that these rationales fail to explicitly describe all important numbers and operations. Their MathQA error analysis also identifies problems with insufficient textual context.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The 2017 AQuA/AQUA-RAT dataset, containing over 100,000 GRE- and GMAT-level multiple-choice math word problems from diverse domains. AQuA problems were expanded through crowdsourcing from 30,000 seed problems and include natural-language rationales.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: To expand annotations, the authors identified closely similar problems using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of four words, replaced numeric values with generic numbers, and extended operation-program annotations to additional AQuA problems.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The authors focused on solvable AQuA problems and removed from consideration non-narrative problems without words and problems requiring brute-force rather than logical reasoning. High-order polynomial problems and problems with entirely nonnumeric solutions were omitted. Problems were categorized using domain-specific n-gram frequencies. MathQA was randomly split into 80% training, 12% development, and 8% testing. For model inputs, arguments were represented by their source: predefined constants, problem numbers ordered by occurrence in the text, and intermediate results ordered by operation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd workers constructed operation programs by iteratively selecting category-specific operations and valid arguments. Operation hints supplied arguments, formulas, and explanations. Valid arguments comprised numbers from the problem, category-specific constants, and previous calculations. Each submitted operation was automatically executed, and its result became an available argument. Final submissions had to use numbers from the problem and produce a value very close to the correct numeric solution. Workers were evaluated using predefined test questions and had to maintain an accuracy threshold; annotations from workers falling below the threshold were marked untrusted and returned to the annotation pool. Three validators assessed alignment between each problem and its program, with at least two required to approve it.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Figure Eight and a custom dynamic annotation platform that provides operation hints, constrains argument selection, calculates intermediate results, and checks final submissions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Programs were accepted when at least two of three validators judged them valid. Validation accuracy was 94.64% across categories. Expert evaluation of 500 problems found 92% of annotations valid and 87% agreement between expert and crowdsourced validation. An experimental automatic dynamic-programming annotation approach achieved only 61% human validation because source rationales were noisy and incomplete; those automatic annotations were excluded. Strategies exposing rationales or end solutions were rejected after manual validation showed that workers constructed programs without reading the problems. For category assessment on 100 problems, human agreement was 84%, and agreement with the automatic category extractor was 74.5%.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Three human validation judgments per operation program; the number of independently authored operation programs per problem is not specified.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A domain-specific category extractor assigns mathematical domain labels using a lexicon of domain-associated n-grams and their frequencies. An automatic dynamic-programming approach to operation-program annotation was tested, but its annotations were excluded from the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset omits high-order polynomials and problems with entirely nonnumeric solutions. Its representation language does not define every needed operation, such as factorization. Domain categorization can be noisy because n-grams may have multiple mathematical interpretations; for example, square and cube can indicate geometry or exponentiation. Some problems have insufficient context or erroneous text. Problems requiring long reasoning chains remain challenging, and sequence problems are identified as a target for future extensions. The paper reports inconsistent dataset totals: approximately 37,200 in the text and 37,259 in Table 1.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of math word problem solvers that map natural-language problems to executable operation programs and select multiple-choice answers. The dataset supports research on domain-aware reasoning and interpretable intermediate solution steps. The authors use an 80% training, 12% development, and 8% testing split.
